Originally introduced in the context of social relationships, the theory posits that the relationship between any two nodes is influenced by their mutual connection to a third node (Heider, 2013; Cartwright and Harary, 1956).
According to the (strong) formulation of structural balance theory, triadic relationships are classified as either balanced or imbalanced (Heider, 2013; Cartwright and Harary, 1956) (Figure 1B).

The strong version, based on the foundational work of Heider and formalized by Cartwright and Harary (Heider, 1946; Heider, 2013; Cartwright and Harary, 1956), posits that the triadic configurations +++ and −+− are structurally balanced, while +−+ and −−− are imbalanced.

By bringing formal network theory (Caplow 1956, 1959; Heider 1958; Simmel 1950) into dialogue with theory on narrative tropes (Townsley 2006) and plot structures (Smith 2005), I elaborate on two triadic tropes that facilitate this narrative shift—those of the “common enemy ” and “mutual friend.”
As Heider (1958) argued, balanced triads are typically perceived as stable and resistant to change.

Heider (1958) argues that in deciding which relationships to build, break, or preserve, people tend to choose options that make their relationships harmonious with those of their friends and oppositional to those of their enemies.

In the next section, I demonstrate how classical triad theory (Caplow 1956, 1959; Heider 1958; Simmel 1950), when reframed through a narrative lens, clarifies how these two triadic tropes function as formal strategies for engaging spectators in international conflicts.

Heider (1958) suggests that these “unbalanced” triads tend to balance over time, as they incentivize people to betray or befriend others for the sake of social stability, whereas balanced triads are more entrenched, as people’s mutual friendships and enmities reinforce their direct relationships.

Simmel ([1908] 2009, 1950) and other network scholars (Caplow 1956, 1959; Heider 1958; Siltaloppi and Vargo 2017) have used this insight to explain how triadic interactions unfold, especially in conflict situations.
